title: Arithmetic on a Column Blocks the Seek
description: Arithmetic on a column (col * 1.1 > x) blocks the index; move the math to the constant side to keep the seek. Why it matters: business calculations (discounts, taxes, totals) routinely end up in WHERE clauses, and this is a common, easy-to-miss way they quietly kill an index.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is a close cousin of the "function on a column" trap, but for arithmetic instead of function calls: doing math on a column *inside* a `WHERE` clause comparison — `WHERE Total * 1.1 > 1500` — quietly disables the index on `Total`, even though the underlying business question ("which orders, after a 10% adjustment, exceed 1500?") is a perfectly ordinary thing to ask.

To see why, go back to what makes an index actually useful: it's a sorted structure containing the *raw* column values — in this case, a sorted list of `Total` values, each pointing back to its row. Because it's sorted, SQL Server can seek — jump almost directly to the right range — as long as the comparison is against the *raw, unmodified* value in that sorted order. The instant you put the column through any kind of calculation before comparing it — multiplying, adding, wrapping it in a function, concatenating it with something else — the thing actually being compared is no longer "the value stored in the index," it's "some newly computed value that only exists after doing math on every row." The index has no pre-computed, sorted list of "what each Total looks like after being multiplied by 1.1" — that number doesn't exist anywhere until SQL Server calculates it, row by row, on demand.

So `WHERE Total * 1.1 > 1500` forces SQL Server to visit every single row, compute `Total * 1.1` for that row, and then check if the result is bigger than 1500 — a full scan, with a multiplication tacked onto every row along the way. This is the concept of a predicate being **non-sargable** ("SARGable" = "Search ARGument-able," meaning the predicate is in a form the engine can directly match against a sorted index to seek). The moment the *column itself* — as opposed to a separate constant — is inside a calculation, that predicate stops being sargable, no matter how good the index on that column is.

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple once you see it, and it's a genuinely universal technique: since basic algebra lets you move terms across an inequality, you can rearrange the math so the column stands completely alone on one side, and all the arithmetic happens only on the constant, which SQL Server can pre-calculate *once*, before the query even starts scanning rows. `Total * 1.1 > 1500` is mathematically identical to `Total > 1500 / 1.1` (roughly `Total > 1363.64`). Rewritten this way, the column `Total` is being compared directly to a single, already-computed number — no math is being done to the column at all — so the index on `Total` works exactly as intended: SQL Server seeks straight to `1363.64` in the sorted index and reads forward from there, matching only the qualifying rows. Same logical result, dramatically cheaper execution, because now the arithmetic happens once (on the constant) instead of once per row (on the column).

It's worth noting this fix isn't always trivially available — some business calculations genuinely can't be rearranged this cleanly (for example, if the calculation combines two *different* columns rather than a column and a constant), and in those trickier cases the more robust long-term fix is often a **computed column** (a column whose value is automatically derived from other columns by a formula you define once) that can itself be indexed, so the calculation is done once at write time instead of on every read. But for the extremely common case of "column compared to a constant after some arithmetic," moving the math to the constant side is usually all it takes.

Why does this matter so much in practice? Because business logic involving money almost always involves some kind of arithmetic — discounts, taxes, markups, thresholds, currency conversions — and it's completely natural for a developer (or a report-writing analyst, or a generated query from a reporting tool) to write the calculation exactly the way they'd say it out loud: "orders where the total plus tax is over 1500." That natural phrasing is exactly the non-sargable shape. Learning to notice "is there math being done to a column inside a WHERE clause?" and instinctively reaching to move that math onto the constant side instead is one of the cheapest, highest-value habits you can build as a developer writing queries against real business data.

It helps to practice the algebra reflex on a few more examples until rearranging feels automatic. `WHERE Price - Discount > 100` becomes `WHERE Price > 100 + Discount` only if `Discount` is a constant, not another column — if it's genuinely another column on the same row, the rearrangement doesn't remove the problem, because now you're comparing one column against another column plus a constant, and neither side is a pure raw column value anymore; this is one of the cases where a computed, indexed column becomes the more robust fix. But for the very common case of "column compared to a constant, with some arithmetic applied to the column," moving the arithmetic to the constant side works cleanly every time and is worth trying first. It's a good general instinct: whenever you see a column on one side of a comparison wrapped in arithmetic, ask "can I use basic algebra to isolate the column completely by itself, moving all the math to the other side?" If yes, that's usually your fastest, simplest fix — no schema changes, no new indexes, just a different (but mathematically identical) way of writing the same condition.

One more thing worth knowing: this same 'move the math to the constant side' technique applies to more than just simple multiplication -- it works for addition, subtraction, and division just as well, as long as the thing being rearranged is a genuine mathematical constant rather than another row-dependent value. The general principle is always the same: isolate the column by itself on one side of the comparison, and let SQL Server pre-compute everything else exactly once.

## Scenario
A report lists orders whose value, after a 10% adjustment, clears a threshold: `WHERE Total * 1.1 > 1500`. `Orders.Total` has a supporting nonclustered index, but the query still **scans** the whole index instead of seeking the range.

## Why it's slow
A predicate is **sargable** (Search-ARGument-able) only when the indexed column stands **alone** on one side of the comparison. The moment you wrap it in an expression — a function like `YEAR(col)` *or* arithmetic like `col * 1.1` — SQL Server must evaluate that expression for **every row** before it can test the predicate. It cannot use the index's sort order to jump to a range, so it falls back to an **Index Scan**.

## What to look for
- The plan reads `IX_Orders_Total` with an **Index Scan** covering all rows.
- Logical reads proportional to the whole table, not the matching slice.

## The concept
Rearrange the algebra so the column is bare and the math lands on the **constant** side. `Total * 1.1 > 1500` is exactly equivalent to `Total > 1500 / 1.1` (≈ 1363.64), which is a clean range the index can **seek**. The result set is identical — only the plan changes. (This is graded on the operator swap and reads because the query returns thousands of rows.)
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE Total * 1.1 > 1500;
hints: The index on Total exists, but the plan is an Index Scan — the predicate isn't sargable.
Total * 1.1 wraps the column in arithmetic, so it must be computed for every row before comparison.
Move the math to the constant side, leaving the column bare: WHERE Total > 1500 / 1.1.
